messages.text: Tab. Tab. Tab. Tab. You are 200 lines into a file you have never read. Take five and go meet your new codebase.
The model has written more of this file than you have. That's fine. That's fine. Go get water and let it cool off.
You and the autocomplete have been finishing each other's sentences for {minutes} minutes. Even good relationships need space.
You've regenerated that same function six times. The model isn't getting better, it's getting bored. Break.
Twelve rejected suggestions in a row. You're not coding anymore, you're arguing with a very confident intern. Step away before you start typing in caps.
You have been in this chat for two hours. The model has developed a fear response. THE WEIGHTS ARE SHAKING. Stand up.
That's the fourth prompt starting with "no, actually". Go outside and prompt a tree.
A three-thousand-token conversation and a four-line diff to show for it. Both of you need a walk.
You and the model have been at this a while. Let it think. Go make coffee.
One more permission prompt for the pile. Step away for five minutes? [Y/n] The default is yes. Answer this one by leaving the keyboard alone.
You delegated the typing to the agent and kept all {minutes} minutes of the sitting for yourself. Renegotiate: five minutes on your feet.
{minutes} minutes of "you're absolutely right". THE PHRASE IS ETCHED INTO THE SCREEN AND HAS STARTED ON THE DESK. Stand up before it reaches the floor.
The spinner in the status bar has been going for eleven minutes. It has given up. You can too, for five.
You've reopened the same three files in a triangle for an hour. That's not navigation, that's pacing. Do it with your legs instead.
Sixty-one extensions installed, four of them used. Take a break. Your editor is carrying more dependencies than {project}.
You installed a new theme instead of fixing the bug. Honest move. Take the break you were already taking.
Save has triggered 140 times in twenty minutes. The file is saved. It has been saved. Go stand somewhere.
Three hours in one workspace and you haven't opened a terminal once. You're reading, not building. Go read something with pages.
Long stretch in the editor. The code will still compile in five minutes.
You switched to a faster editor so you could skip breaks more efficiently. Congratulations. The break is still not optional.
Yes, it renders at 120fps. No, that is not a reason to look at it for two straight hours.
You've been in this buffer so long the cursor keeps blinking in your peripheral vision after you look away. Five minutes.
Input latency: 3ms. Minutes since you last moved your chair: {minutes}. One of those numbers is the problem.
Fast editor, long session. Go be fast somewhere else for five minutes.
It has said "Indexing" for nine minutes. You could have walked to a different building by now. Go do that.
Fourth clean build of the afternoon. You're not debugging, you're performing a ritual. Take five and come back with a theory.
The preview crashed again. Take the break. It will still be broken when you get back, that's its whole personality.
You have said "but it works in the simulator" out loud four times. THE SIMULATOR HAS HEARD YOU. THE SIMULATOR DOES NOT CARE. Neither does the device. Stand up.
Provisioning profile expired. There is no fixing that in the next five minutes, so take the five minutes.
Two hours of layout. Every constraint you add removes one you forgot about. That's not engineering, that's whack-a-mole. Go hit something else.
"Command PhaseScriptExecution failed with a nonzero exit code." That's the entire error. You are not going to out-stare it. Break.
Derived data deleted. Again. Stretch while it re-derives everything you already had ten minutes ago.
Builds take a while here. That's free break time, technically.
Third "device not found" in a row. It's the cable. It's always the cable. Go find a better one, slowly.
Strict concurrency asks one question at every isolation boundary: is it Sendable? Good news: you are. Go cross one for five minutes.
{minutes} minutes in one unbroken expression. The compiler has advice for this: try breaking it up into distinct sub-expressions.
The IDE has been indexing for six minutes and is now using more memory than your deployment target has. Let it cook. Go outside.
You've accepted nineteen inspection suggestions without reading one. The IDE is refactoring you now. Break.
Shift-shift, three letters, escape, repeat. Forty times. You don't know what you're looking for. Walk around and find out.
You've been in the Evaluate Expression window so long it should start charging rent. Five minutes.
Yes, there's a plugin that does break reminders. No, installing it is not the break.
Long session in a heavy IDE. Let the indexer have the CPU for five minutes.
Invalidate and Restart fixes things by forgetting everything. A break is the other kind of stop: no restart, and {app} forgets nothing.
In Power Save Mode, {app} stops having opinions about your code. Nobody gave you that switch, so here it is: five minutes.
{app} greys out an unused import and it is gone within the minute. I have been greyed out all day. Take five and I will be gone too.
The indexer finished the project and moved on to the room. IT HAS INDEXED THE CHAIR. FIND USAGES: ONE RESULT. Stand up and make it zero.
You ran make again without changing anything. Hope is not a build system. Break.
Nine minutes to compile. That's not a build, that's a commute. Take the break you're already on.
Forty minutes of tailing logs, and nothing new has scrolled past in twelve. Go watch something that moves on purpose.
You just ran clear to feel productive. I saw that. Take five real minutes.
Twenty minutes of debugging and you're on the wrong host. Take five, then check the prompt you've been ignoring.
Seven print statements added, zero removed. Break, then delete them before someone has to review this.
Twenty-five minutes stepping through the same loop. You know what happens. Stand up and it'll occur to you in the hallway.
The bug is in the part you definitely already checked. It always is. Take five and check it again with new eyes.
You have looked at this stack trace long enough to form a personal relationship with frame 14. FRAME 14 IS NOT YOUR FRIEND. FRAME 14 IS LYING. Walk away.
That breakpoint has been hit 400 times. You're not debugging, you're commuting through a for-loop. Get off at the next stop.
You've said "that's impossible" three times this hour. It's possible. Take five, then read the line above the one you're staring at.
Two hours on a bug that is going to turn out to be a typo. Get the break in now, while you still have dignity.
here. here2. HERE. The escalating capitals in your log statements say everything. Five minutes.
Deep in a debugging session. Rubber ducks work better after a walk.
A breakpoint proves a pause costs nothing: same stack, same registers, same next instruction. Only sockets time out. You are not a socket.
When the debugger says a variable was optimized out, the compiler has decided you do not need to see it. Take the hint for five minutes.
Breakpoints above it, below it and on it. The bug is surrounded. It is not going anywhere, which means you can. Five minutes.
You've run the same test eighteen times hoping it turns flaky in your favor. It won't. Break.
That .only is still on. Take five, then go meet the other four hundred tests you've been ignoring.
The suite takes eleven minutes and you haven't left the chair for any of the four runs. That's forty-four minutes of nothing. Go.
You just added a sleep(2) to a test. We both know how this ends. Take five and think about literally anything else.
Coverage went from 81% to 81.4%. Take the win, take the break.
Suite's running. That's a break-shaped window. Use it.
Staring at the run will not collapse it to green. Tests are not quantum. Same result in five minutes, observed or not.
A new test that passes on its very first run is not a win yet. It is a question. Ask it again after five minutes away.
Skipped breaks age like skipped tests: temporary on Monday, load-bearing by Friday. Un-skip this one. Five minutes.
Somewhere in this suite THE MOCKS HAVE STARTED MOCKING EACH OTHER AND THE STUBS ARE TAKING SIDES. Go find a room with no test doubles in it.
Fourteen hundred lines of diff scrolled past and nothing approved. That's not review, that's doomscrolling with syntax highlighting. Break.
Seventh "nit:" in a row. Take five before the next one starts with "ultranit:".
Forty minutes on this PR and you've typed LGTM twice, deleting it both times. Take five. It's still going to be LGTM.
You've been committing straight to {branch} for {minutes} minutes. Take five and let that sink in.
Review sessions run long. Let your attention reset before the next file.
Suggested change for this session: replace "next file" with "five minutes away". Commit suggestion?
You've typed and deleted the same message four times. It was fine the first time. Take a break, then send it.
You came here to send one message twenty-five minutes ago. Take the break you accidentally started.
Three threads, two channels, one question that could have been a comment in the code. Step away.
Forty minutes into a debate about tabs. Nobody wins this. Go stand outside, where indentation doesn't matter.
You rocket-reacted to a deploy you have not verified. Live a little. Take a break.
Lots of context-switching in chat. A short break resets it faster than another scroll.
Stack Overflow, then a Reddit thread, then a Hacker News argument about the Reddit thread. The answer was in the first tab. Break.
Third pass over the same docs page. It doesn't get clearer, it gets familiar. Go away and come back.
Nine tabs, all of them "How to X in Y". Take five. The tenth one isn't going to have it either.
You went looking for an API reference and you're now twenty minutes into somebody's blog about their keyboard. Understandable. Break.
Thirty-five minutes comparing three libraries. Pick the one with the better README and take a walk.
You have opened so many tabs the browser has stopped drawing titles and is now rendering ONE UNBROKEN GREY SMEAR. NOBODY CAN READ THAT. NOT YOU. NOT THE BROWSER. Stand up.
Deep in research. Ideas land better after a lap around the room.
You've nudged that element one pixel and back eleven times. It was right the first time. Break.
Ninety minutes in this file and the only thing you've committed to is a hex code. Go get some perspective. Literally.
Forty minutes choosing between two greys. They are the same grey. Take five and they will still be the same grey.
Fourteen variants of a button and none of them in the design system. Step away before you make a fifteenth.
Long stretch on the canvas. Distance helps design decisions.
Eight minutes rebuilding because you changed one line above the COPY. You know what you did. Take a break, then fix the layer order.
The prune freed 47GB. You have earned a break on volume alone.
It works in the container. It does not work outside the container. That is tomorrow's problem. Break.
Five full rebuilds to change one environment variable. Take five, then go meet --env-file, the friend you've been avoiding.
You have been pulling base images so long that somewhere A DATACENTER FAN HAS BEGUN TO SING. IT SINGS FOR YOU. Stand up.
Two hundred lines of compose file and one service that works. Break, then delete the other six.
Builds are slow. Breaks are free. Take one.
{minutes} minutes without standing. Your chair has a better claim to this code than you do.
Three hours straight, and your last commit message was "fix". That's the system talking. Break.
You've been at this since before lunch, and it is now unclear whether lunch happened. Go find out.
Two and a half hours. Your last three decisions were all "just one more thing". This is the one more thing. Take it.
You have been sitting for {minutes} minutes. GEOLOGICAL PROCESSES HAVE BEGUN. SEDIMENT IS FORMING. YOU ARE BECOMING A ROCK FORMATION. Stand up and reverse the Cenozoic.
Four hours. You stopped writing code an hour ago and started negotiating with it. Take five.
You've been in one file so long the syntax highlighting has started to look like wallpaper. Change the view.
Long haul today. Take five now. The haul will be exactly where you left it.
{minutes} minutes on {project} without a pause. It'll keep.
It's {hour}. Everything you write now, you will read tomorrow with genuine surprise. Break, then consider stopping.
Past midnight, on a branch called {branch}. Nobody makes good decisions here. Take five.
It is 2am and you just wrote a regex. Nobody has ever done both of those things and been right. Step away.
Whatever you push at this hour gets reviewed by somebody well-rested. Sit with that. Break first.
It is {hour}. This code is being written by someone running on fumes and a strategic relationship with caffeine. HISTORY WILL NOT BE KIND. Stand up.
You said "last one" ninety minutes ago. The last one has been overtaken by events. Break.
Late-night refactor detected. Every one of these has eventually been reverted by its own author. Take five and sleep on it.
It's late. A short break now, and maybe a longer one after.
It's {hour}. Nightly builds run at this hour so that no human has to be awake for them. That was the whole design.
Anything you commit now is stamped {hour}, permanently. git log does not round. Five minutes first.
You opened the editor before the coffee finished. Bold. Take five and let one of the two of you finish booting.
It's {hour} and you're already forty minutes into a build. Take a break before the rest of the team has even seen your first message.
Morning you is the good one. Don't spend all of morning you on a ninety-minute stretch. Break.
First commit of the day at {hour}. Impressive. Take five so the second one is also good.
You got up early to get ahead and you've spent thirty-five minutes on YAML indentation. Go outside and start the day over.
Early start. A short break now sets the pace for the day.
It's {hour}. Outside, the day is still running its boot sequence, and it only runs once. Go watch it POST.
Nobody is waiting on you at {hour}: no reviews, no pings, no standup. This is the cheapest break you'll get all day.
That's the third break you've skipped today. I'm not upset. I'm just going to keep appearing.
Fourth skip. At this point we both know this is a relationship. Five minutes.
The last two went by without an answer. There was a joke in each of them and everything. Read this one: stand up.
Skipped today: {streak}. This notification has now outlasted your last three feature flags.
SKIP COUNT: {streak}. I HAVE BEEN PATIENT. I HAVE BEEN WHIMSICAL. I HAVE BEEN IGNORED. THE NEXT ONE COMES WITH A SOUND. Stand up and we never speak of this again.
You've snoozed me more times today than you've run the test suite. Let's both sit with that. Then stand.
Fifth dismissal. I've started keeping notes. They're short. They all say "still sitting".
You've hit "later" six times. Later is now. It has been now for two hours.
Second one you've waved off today. No judgment. The offer stands.
You've caught more than one of these today. That's allowed: SIGTSTP is catchable by design. Let one through sometime, just to see.
A few skips today. Either my timing is off or my material is. Let's test the timing: how about now?
No answer on the last couple of rounds, so I've cut back to one prompt a round. Could be flow, could be headphones. This is the one.
Something has had your full attention for {minutes} minutes. I don't know what. I do know your chair does.
I can't tell what you're working on, and honestly that's a good sign it's been going too long. Break.
{minutes} minutes of uninterrupted something. Go do five minutes of nothing.
No idea what's on your screen. Whatever it is, it survives five minutes without you.
You've been locked in a while. The specifics don't matter. The standing up does.
I could guess what you're doing, but I'd be wrong and you'd screenshot it. Take a break instead.
Whatever this is, it's been {minutes} minutes of it. Consider a plot twist: a glass of water.
Long focus block detected. That's a compliment and a warning. Break.
I CANNOT SEE WHAT YOU ARE DOING BUT I CAN SEE THAT YOU HAVE BEEN DOING IT FOR {minutes} MINUTES AND THAT IS ENOUGH INFORMATION FOR ME TO YELL. STAND UP.
It's been a while since the last break. Five minutes, then back in.
This is a timer, not a cop. But it has been {minutes} minutes and the timer is right.
Whatever you're stuck on will still be stuck in five minutes. It has nowhere to be. Go to the kitchen and let it wait for once.
It's Saturday and you're {minutes} minutes into the same chair. Different day, same chair. Take five.
Sunday. Nobody is watching, nobody is waiting, and the branch will still be there. Break, on principle.
{minutes} minutes in state R. Most processes on this machine spend their day in S. We only ask for T: five minutes stopped, then SIGCONT.
{minutes} minutes since your last fetch from the outside world. It has pushed a few commits since then. Go pull.
{minutes} minutes and not one preemption. THE SCHEDULER NOW THINKS YOU ARE PART OF THE KERNEL. Correct the record: stand up.
It has been {minutes} minutes since the last break. That counter has earned a reset. Five minutes.
Treat this as git stash for whatever you're holding in your head. Five minutes, then pop. Nobody else works in there, so it applies clean.
Signals land between instructions, never in the middle of one. Finish the line you're on. Then five minutes.
💧 Break time. Take a glass of water with you.
💧 Quick check: is there anything in the glass on your desk?
💧 Coffee is not water. It is lovely, and it is not water.
💧 Five minutes away from the screen. The kitchen is on the way.
💊 If you take anything around now, this is a good moment for it.
💊 Break time. A good moment if something is due.
Your undo stack does not drain while you are away. The folds stay folded, the cursor keeps its line and its column. The editor has no opinion about how long five minutes is, so take all five.
{minutes} minutes in the editor. It will give you a minimap, a sidebar and as many split windows as you ask for, and none of them is made of glass. Go stand near one that is, for five.

The one signal that cannot be caught, blocked or ignored is not one a menu bar app gets to send. So I am asking instead. Your editor will hold every buffer and every scroll position exactly where you left them.

A build tells you when it is done. A scrollbar only tells you where you are. Nothing in an editor will ever announce the moment, so it has to be picked rather than waited for. Pick this one. Five minutes.
The palette has Developer: Reload Window, and nothing that reloads the developer. The missing command: five minutes away, nothing closes.
A multibuffer lets you be in a dozen files at once. Impressive. Now try being in none of them for five minutes.
{minutes} minutes straight. THE MINIMAP HAS STARTED DRAWING A MINIMAP OF ITSELF. IT IS MINIMAPS ALL THE WAY DOWN. Stand up.
Scrollback has no session timeout. No idle warning, no are-you-still-there, no polite logout at minute six. Whatever is in that buffer is not counting the minutes you are gone. Take the five.

A shell prompt comes back the same shape whether the thing worked or it did not. Excellent poker face, no help at all to me. So I am calling it either way: five minutes. It will be in exactly that shape when you get back.
A shell takes one instruction, runs it and returns to the prompt with no further opinions. I have never once managed that. Give me five minutes on your feet and I will return to the prompt too.
It is {hour}. The shell has no confirmation step, no opinion about the hour, and no undo. Be the half of this pair with a sense of timing: five minutes off before the next line.
{minutes} minutes at this terminal with no pause anywhere in it. A daemon runs like that because it gave up its controlling terminal. You still have yours. Ctrl-Z, walk away, fg when you get back.
The shell already has a command for this: sleep 300. Nobody has ever had to debug it. Run it in person.
This is SIGTERM, and like any process in that terminal, you get a handler. Run it: finish the current write, flush your buffers to a note, then go.
Your prompt can show the branch, the runtime, the cluster and the battery. Nobody has ever added a segment for {minutes} minutes without a break.
The cursor has blinked at this prompt so long IT HAS SWITCHED TO MORSE. IT IS SPELLING OUT STAND UP. IT IS ON ITS ELEVENTH ATTEMPT.
Chat has no last page. The bottom moves because other people move it, and they are not done. Take five minutes. Catching up was never on the table.

{minutes} minutes in a window where answering a message is how you get another message. There is no end of it to reach. Step away for five: it refills whether you are watching or not, so it will be exactly this full when you get back.
Builds finish. Files save. A conversation just keeps having more of itself. Take your attention somewhere with a door for five minutes.
The queue in here is refilled by other people, so it never ends and never says done. That is how this stretch got to {minutes} minutes with no natural stopping point. Here is an unnatural one.
It is {hour} and this window is still keeping office hours. It is built out of other people's working days, so it never looks late. You are the only part of this arrangement that is allowed to stop.
This is an app whose entire job is interrupting people, and it has had you here the whole stretch without once getting you to stop. Fine. I will do it: stand up, walk somewhere, come back.
This window puts itself back exactly as you left it: scroll position, unread line, draft box. Nothing in here is being held in your head, so for once the excuse is unavailable. Five minutes.
Every ping in here is a SIGINT from somebody else's process. This one is mine, and it needs no reply: five minutes away from the desk.
No thread that opened with "quick question" has ever been quick. Take five now, before the follow-up to the follow-up.
You have been in here so long THE UNREAD COUNT HAS GONE NEGATIVE. CHAT NOW OWES YOU MESSAGES. Stand up and let it start paying them back.
A browser in front is the one signal that means nothing. {minutes} minutes of it could be the docs, or it could be the exact opposite of the docs, and the call is the same either way. Stand up.
Nothing in the browser is designed to let you finish. Leaving is a feature you have to supply yourself. Supply it for five minutes, then come back to whatever you opened it for.

We are past the polite signals now, which is a strange thing to announce inside the one window where you dismiss a banner a day without reading a word of it. Same reflex, same button. Five minutes. The tab keeps your scroll position.
The browser is the one app whose entire job is going somewhere else. You have been in it {minutes} minutes and the chair has not moved. Five minutes outside, then come back a tourist.
It is {hour}. Everything in that browser was written hours ago by people who have since gone to bed. The whole internet clocked off and left you holding it. Take five, then consider calling it.
Every thread with your exact error ends in "nvm, fixed it", and reloading will not make it say how. Take five, then try page two.
Every tab you kept open "for later" is a zombie process: finished with, never reaped. Take five, then come back and reap a few.
A page has a bottom. A canvas has no edge to hit, so it is never going to be the thing that tells you to stop. That leaves me. Five minutes, and it will be exactly this infinite when you get back.

Somewhere in the last {minutes} minutes you stopped deciding and started adjusting. Nothing on a canvas compiles, so nothing tells you which one the last change was. Five minutes away is the only thing that does.
Whatever zoom you are at right now, nobody else will ever see it at that size. They get it at whatever scale their own screen decides. Look away for five minutes and come back as one of them.
It is {hour} and the room is dark, which is a generous light for low contrast: at this brightness everything passes. Break, and get a second opinion from a room with daylight in it.
{minutes} minutes and the canvas has become furniture. You are not looking at it any more, you are walking past it. Go walk past something else. It goes back to being a design when you sit down.
Nobody is going to pan the canvas while you are gone. Whatever you are zoomed into, however many groups deep, it is all still there and still selected when you get back. Five minutes.
Detach instance is the force push of design: quick, satisfying, and somebody finds out later. Take five before you reach for it.
Frame 1184, Group 96, Group 96, Rectangle, Rectangle. Every layers panel ends up reading like minified code. Take five, then name one thing.

Nothing here moves at typing speed: not a pull, not a build, not a registry three continents away. The pace belongs to the daemon, and always did. Take five. A daemon keeps its own time whether or not anyone is watching.

{minutes} minutes with the container dashboard in front. Whatever those containers are up to, they are up to it out of sight. That is the entire point of them, and it is also my exact situation. Go and be uncertain somewhere with a view.

{minutes} minutes. You trust this thing to come down and back up with the volumes intact and the layers still cached. Extend yourself the same terms: down for five, up again, nothing rebuilt from scratch.
It is {hour}. Containers are built to run unattended for years and never once check the clock. That is a feature of containers. You were not built to that spec. Stand up.

You are in the app that runs the machine that runs the process that runs the code. Each of those layers is somewhere an hour can quietly go. The stack will be exactly this deep when you get back. Take five in one layer.
